title: Alcohol withdrawal and delirium tremens
subject: psychiatry
setting: Emergency department, ward, ICU, de-addiction centre
summary: Grade severity with CIWA-Ar and treat with benzodiazepines, preferably symptom-triggered (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; lorazepam in liver disease or the elderly). Give parenteral thiamine to prevent or treat Wernicke encephalopathy, and manage delirium tremens with IV benzodiazepines in a monitored setting (ASAM 2020, NICE CG100).

sections.title: Recognise
items: Withdrawal starts 6 to 24 hours after the last drink: tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea, insomnia, tachycardia and hypertension.
Withdrawal seizures are usually generalised and occur within 48 hours; alcoholic hallucinosis occurs with a clear sensorium.
Delirium tremens (usually 48 to 96 hours): fluctuating confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, severe agitation, autonomic hyperactivity and fever. It is life-threatening.

Higher risk of severe or complicated withdrawal: previous delirium or seizures, many previous withdrawals, CIWA-Ar 10 or more at presentation, serious medical illness, older age, long heavy drinking, other sedative dependence.
Exclude mimics and co-existing illness: hypoglycaemia, head injury (subdural haematoma), sepsis or meningitis, hepatic encephalopathy, Wernicke encephalopathy, other drug withdrawal or intoxication.

sections.title: Assessment and investigations
items: CIWA-Ar (10 items, maximum 67): below 10 mild, 10 to 18 moderate, 19 or more severe (ASAM). Reassess regularly, more often when scores are high.
CIWA-Ar needs a patient who can communicate; in delirium use a sedation scale (RASS) or delirium tool (CAM-ICU) instead.
Glucose, electrolytes including magnesium, phosphate and potassium, liver function, INR, renal function, CBC, and blood alcohol if available.
CT head after a first seizure, focal signs, head injury, or an atypical or prolonged course.

sections.title: Thiamine and supportive care
items: Thiamine for everyone in withdrawal: 100 mg IV or IM daily for 3 to 5 days (ASAM), IV preferred if malnourished or withdrawal is severe; then oral thiamine.

Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, or unexplained coma or hypothermia in a drinker): high-dose IV thiamine, 200 to 500 mg every 8 hours, for at least 5 days (NICE), then oral.
Thiamine and glucose can be given in any order or together (ASAM 2020): never delay glucose for hypoglycaemia; where practical give thiamine before or with dextrose-containing fluids.
Correct magnesium, phosphate and potassium; IV fluids for dehydration; nutrition; a calm, well-lit room with close observation.

sections.title: Benzodiazepine regimens
items: Symptom-triggered dosing is preferred in hospital or wherever 24-hour monitoring is available (NICE, ASAM): give a dose when CIWA-Ar is 10 or more and reassess after about 1 hour.
Chlordiazepoxide (ASAM examples): mild 25 to 50 mg, moderate 50 to 100 mg, severe 75 to 100 mg orally; symptom-triggered 25 to 100 mg every 4 to 6 hours when CIWA-Ar is 10 or more.

Fixed-dose taper when symptom-triggered monitoring is not possible: for example chlordiazepoxide 25 to 100 mg every 4 to 6 hours on day 1, reducing the daily total by 25 to 50% per day over 3 to 5 days, with extra doses if needed.
Severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar 19 or more): front-load with diazepam or chlordiazepoxide, for example diazepam 10 to 20 mg or chlordiazepoxide 50 to 100 mg every 1 to 2 hours until CIWA-Ar is below 10.
Cirrhosis, the elderly or respiratory disease: prefer a benzodiazepine with less hepatic metabolism (lorazepam or oxazepam), with a gradual taper and close watch for oversedation.
Withdrawal seizure: a quick-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam 2 mg IV reduces recurrence. Do not use phenytoin (NICE, ASAM).

If benzodiazepines are contraindicated in mild to moderate withdrawal: carbamazepine (600 to 800 mg/day, tapering over 4 to 9 days) or gabapentin. Phenobarbital only by experienced clinicians with close monitoring.
Stop benzodiazepines at the end of the withdrawal course; do not continue long term.

sections.title: Delirium tremens
items: Manage in HDU or ICU with close nursing observation; sedate to light somnolence. NICE: oral lorazepam first line; parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol if symptoms persist or oral treatment is refused.
Use IV benzodiazepine boluses by an established protocol, for example lorazepam 1 to 4 mg IV or diazepam 10 to 20 mg IV, repeated every few minutes until calm. Very large doses may be needed.

Resistant withdrawal (poor control despite about 150 to 200 mg diazepam or 30 to 40 mg lorazepam in 3 to 4 hours): add phenobarbital in a monitored setting (for example 10 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes); propofol or dexmedetomidine for intubated patients.
Antipsychotics (for example haloperidol) only as an adjunct for hallucinations or agitation not controlled by benzodiazepines, never alone, as they lower the seizure threshold.
Do not use beta-blockers, clonidine or paraldehyde to treat delirium tremens.
Watch for respiratory depression, aspiration, hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis with repeated high IV doses; use restraints only to prevent injury.

sections.title: Admission and discharge
items: Admit for delirium tremens, seizures, severe withdrawal, high-risk features, significant medical or psychiatric illness, or no reliable supervision; use a lower threshold for frail or vulnerable people (NICE).
Mild, low-risk withdrawal can be managed in the community with daily review and a limited supply. Advise dependent drinkers not to stop suddenly without medical support.
Before discharge: brief intervention, referral to de-addiction services, and consider relapse prevention medicines (for example acamprosate or naltrexone) with psychosocial support.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using CIWA-Ar in a patient who cannot communicate or has delirium from another cause.
Missing Wernicke encephalopathy (the full triad is often absent) or giving only low-dose oral thiamine.
Phenytoin for withdrawal seizures.
Oversedation from accumulating long-acting benzodiazepines in cirrhosis or the elderly.
Labelling fever and confusion as delirium tremens without excluding sepsis, meningitis or head injury.

drugs.name: Chlordiazepoxide
drugs.dose: 25 to 100 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours when CIWA-Ar is 10 or more; front-loading 50 to 100 mg every 1 to 2 hours in severe withdrawal
drugs.notes: Avoid in decompensated liver disease; taper over 3 to 5 days if fixed dosing.

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mg orally or IV, every 1 to 2 hours until CIWA-Ar below 10 (front-loading)
drugs.notes: Long-acting; accumulates in cirrhosis and the elderly.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 1 to 4 mg orally, IM or IV per dose; 2 mg IV after a withdrawal seizure
drugs.notes: Preferred in liver disease; first line for delirium tremens (NICE).

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.dose: Prophylaxis 100 mg IV or IM daily for 3 to 5 days; suspected Wernicke 200 to 500 mg IV every 8 hours for at least 5 days
drugs.notes: Then oral thiamine; do not delay glucose for it.

drugs.name: Phenobarbital
drugs.dose: 10 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes as an adjunct
drugs.notes: Resistant withdrawal, monitored setting, experienced clinicians only.

drugs.name: Carbamazepine
drugs.dose: 600 to 800 mg/day orally, tapering to 200 to 400 mg/day over 4 to 9 days
drugs.notes: Alternative for mild to moderate withdrawal when benzodiazepines are contraindicated.

sources.title: The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management
Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications (CG100)
